messages.content: I know what a Python list is. I don't know what happens when two keys land in the same dict bucket. One picture.

<think>
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=teach|construct=teacher|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
They already have the list. The gap is the bucket. A dict is a list of buckets. The hash picks the bucket. Equality picks the key inside a small chain in that bucket. If I only had equality I would scan the whole collection. The picture is a row of boxes, two names in one box, and a short walk of that box only.
</think>

A dict is a row of boxes. The hash picks the box. If two keys share a box, they sit in a short chain, and lookup walks that chain checking equality. Hash chooses the box. Equality chooses the key inside it.
I know what a git commit is. I don't know what a rebase does to commits that already exist. Teach that, not the whole of git.

<think>
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=teach|construct=teacher|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
Start from the commit they know. Rebase does not edit that object. It copies the changes onto a new parent, and the copy has a new id. The old commit remains until nothing points at it. That is why rebasing a branch someone else already pulled rewrites history they have.
</think>

Rebase copies your commits onto a new base. The new commits have new ids. The old ones are still in the object store until nothing points at them. That is why rebasing a branch someone else has already pulled rewrites the history they have.
I can write a SQL WHERE. Why doesn't the index get used when I wrap the column in LOWER? One concrete reason.

<think>
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=teach|construct=teacher|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
They know the WHERE. The gap is what the index is sorted by. It is sorted by the raw column. LOWER(email) is a different sequence, so the sorted list can't be walked. The fix is an index on the expression, or a comparison that doesn't wrap the column.
</think>

The index is sorted by the raw email. LOWER(email) is a different value, so the planner can't walk that sorted list. Index the expression, or compare the column without wrapping it.
I know what a function is. I don't know why an idempotency key has to be written down before the call, not after. Explain it with a timeout.

<think>
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=teach|construct=teacher|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
The failure they need is the timeout after success. The charge happens, the response dies, the worker thinks it failed, and a flag written after the response never got written. The key has to exist before the call so the retry can show the same key and get the original result back.
</think>

If the charge succeeds and the response times out, your code thinks it failed. A flag you meant to write after the response never gets written. The key has to be stored before the call, so the retry can send the same key and get the original charge back instead of a second one.
Teach me what p95 means. I know an average. Use the search page, which is usually fast and sometimes awful.

<think>
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=teach|construct=teacher|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
Average hides the awful tail. Sort the latencies, take the point where 95% are faster. One slow request in a hundred barely moves the average and is the whole p95 story if the tail is long. On the search page, p95 is the slow experience a real person actually hits, not the typical one.
</think>

Sort a hundred search latencies. p95 is the 95th, the point where only five were slower. The average can stay small while that 95th is awful, which is why the page feels fast to you and broken to someone else.
I understand a boolean. I don't understand why 'if value:' is the wrong test when value is a quantity that is allowed to be zero. Show it.

<think>
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=teach|construct=teacher|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
They know if. The gap is that zero is a real quantity and is falsy. A missing quantity and a quantity of zero fall in the same branch. The test they want is 'is value None', or they should use a sentinel that isn't a legal amount.
</think>

Zero is a real quantity, and `if value` treats it as missing. A cart with quantity 0 and a cart where quantity was never set take the same branch. Test `value is None` if zero is allowed.
